content.text:
## What I found: tools and durability

- **The builder can't read everything chat can.** It has 7 read sources. Chat can also read transaction details, entity lists, what-if scenarios, forecasts, wealth (money lent and owed), and agent findings. Net worth history has no tool anywhere, even though Home shows it.
- **It isn't truly durable.** The build runs in `after()` inside one function call with a 300s limit:
  - Closing the tab works only while that call stays alive. A deploy, crash or timeout loses the build, and it gets marked "failed" 6 minutes later.
  - It never retries.
  - When you come back you see only "running". The steps it already showed are gone.

**Fix:**
- **Move the builder to Vercel Workflow.** The repo already uses it for reviews, bank sync and imports. Each model call or tool call becomes a checkpointed step that retries on its own. Progress goes to the workflow stream, and `getRun(id).getReadable({ startIndex })` lets any tab reconnect and replay from the start, even after closing the site.
- **One shared read-only tool registry** used by chat, the artifact builder and the widget renderer. Any read tool added to chat automatically becomes available to artifacts. Net worth history and budgets get added as new sources.

## The core idea

An artifact becomes **one agent conversation that owns two outputs**:

- **The Page:** free HTML in a sandbox, as today, with a better default design.
- **The Home card:** rendered natively in the app.

The same chat edits either one, and the agent works out which from what you say ("show this as well on Home" changes the card). Each output keeps its own version history with undo.

## How the Home card renders: three tiers, chosen by the AI

| Tier | What the AI produces | Runs where | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. Preset** | One of the 6 templates plus data links | Our React, on the server | Most cards |
| **2. Composed** | A JSON layout built from ~20 of our primitives (Stack, Row, Stat, Delta, BarList, LineChart, AreaChart, Donut, Heatmap, Table, Progress, Badge, Segmented, Select, Tabs, Empty…) | Our React, on the server | Cards that don't fit a preset. This is the "AI makes its own template" case, and it's still 100% native. |
| **3. React code** | TSX written by the AI, using our component kit | **Sandboxed iframe** with our real CSS, fonts and components loaded, at a fixed size | Truly bespoke visuals |

**On "it can make React code":** yes, but never running inside the app itself. Code there would have your session, so a bad generation or an instruction hidden in a transaction description could call any server action (move money, delete data). Tier 3 gets the native look by loading the same component kit inside the sandbox. In practice Tier 2 should cover almost everything; Tier 3 is the escape hatch.

**Tier choice:** the agent tries the tiers in order (preset, then composed, then code) and picks the first that fits the request. All tiers share one data contract.

## Interactivity on Home

- **Params.** A card can declare controls such as month, period (1M/3M/6M) or account. A change calls `GET /api/widgets/:id?month=2026-10`. The server checks the value against the declared allowed values, re-runs that card's queries, and re-renders it. Nothing is computed by the AI at view time.
- **Local interactions** need no server call: tabs between series already loaded, tooltips, hover.
- **Drill-through links.** Clicking a bar can open `/money/transactions?category=…`. Links can only go to an allowlist of app routes, which iframes can't do today.
- **Tier 3** gets the same params through `postMessage`, so the app stays in control of data.

## Data contract (how financial truth is kept)

- Each card stores its own **queries**, using the shared registry and rolling forward with time as today. Changing the Page never breaks the card.
- Data is linked to the card with **paths plus a small set of safe operations** (`top n`, `sum`, `share`, `delta vs previous`). These run in app code on bigint minor units, with no `eval`. The app does all money formatting.
- **Checked before saving:** the agent's draft runs against live data in a step. Every link must resolve, the text must fit the chosen size (an overflow check from a server render), and empty or error states must be defined. A failed check goes back to the agent with the error, up to N times.

## Architecture

**Durable agent (Workflow `artifactAgent`):**
- Each turn starts a run: load the thread, call the model in a loop, run tools as steps, save.
- Tools:
  - every shared read tool
  - `write_page(html, queries)`
  - `write_card(tier, spec | tsx, queries, params, sizes)`
  - `check_card` (runs it live and reports the check results)
  - `ask_user` (clarifying questions)
- Progress events go to the workflow stream, so you can reconnect from anywhere. A small "Building…" pill in the app shell shows runs still active.

**Data model (fresh tables, no migration of old artifacts):**
- `artifacts`: id, title, thread state
- `artifact_messages`: the chat
- `artifact_pages`: versioned HTML and queries
- `artifact_cards`: versioned tier, spec/tsx, queries, params, allowed sizes, default size
- `artifact_runs`: workflow run id and status
- Home layout entries become `{ key, size }`, so built-in cards can be resized too. A pinned card points at a specific card version: chat edits create drafts, and **"Update on Home"** publishes one, so Home never changes without you seeing the change.

**Rendering:**
- `lib/widgets/primitives/*` is the component catalog. It is used both by the native renderer and, bundled, as the Tier 3 sandbox kit.
- `lib/widgets/spec.ts` holds the Zod schemas for Tiers 1–2, sizes and params.
- Home renders cards inside Suspense on the server. Tier 3 cards render as fixed-size frames. Sizes are fixed grid slots (S 2×1, M 3×1, L 4×1, XL 6×1) with a fixed height and no scrolling.
- The preview in the artifact's "Home card" tab uses **the same Home grid component** with your real neighbouring cards, so what you see is exactly what you get.

**Page design:**
- A **Moneo kit** is injected into the sandbox: CSS classes for cards, stats, eyebrows and grids, chart colours, and a chart helper.
- Default prompt: "use the kit unless the user asks for a specific style". When the user asks for a style, it wins.
- The Mercury design text in the examples gets removed.

## Build order (each phase a few commits)

1. Shared read-tool registry and the missing sources.
2. Builder on Workflow with a resumable stream, plus the chat thread and new tables.
3. Primitives, the Tier 1 and 2 renderer, fixed sizes and layout `{key, size}`.
4. The Home card tab, live preview, draft and publish.
5. Params, server re-render and drill-through links.
6. The Page design kit and prompt.
7. The Tier 3 sandbox with the bundled kit (optional, last).

## Decisions I need from you

1. **Tier 3 React code:** include it in the first version, or ship Tiers 1–2 first and add it only if we hit a real gap? I'd ship 1–2 first.
2. **Updating Home:** chat edits stay as drafts until you press "Update on Home", or go straight to Home? I'd use drafts.
3. **Multiple cards per artifact:** allow it (e.g. a "Subscriptions" artifact giving a total card and a next-charges card), or one card each? I'd allow several, since it costs little in this design.

content.thinking:
I'm weighing whether dropping Tier 2 and jumping straight to Tier 3 React code is actually better — the tradeoff is losing native-feeling UI since AI-generated React would need to run in a sandboxed iframe on Home, which has real performance costs. I'm considering an alternative: rendering that React code server-side only, producing static HTML in an isolated runtime, so no AI-authored client JS ever executes directly in the user's browser.

This feels promising: render the AI component inside a sandboxed VM server-side into an HTML string using our own primitives, sanitize it, then inject it natively into the page with our Tailwind classes — no iframe, same DOM, full native look. Interactivity would work through declared params triggering server re-renders, charts would be SVG rendered server-side, and limited client interactions like tooltips could be handled generically via data attributes and our own client-side code. The real tradeoffs are needing a genuine sandbox runtime since node:vm isn't a real security boundary, and the added rendering overhead on each Home load.

Weighing this against the simpler iframe approach, the iframe route gives full native-feeling interactivity (hover states, local component state) and is already proven since artifact frames exist, but comes with per-card iframe overhead, fixed sizing requirements, and theming friction. Given the user's actual question about whether to keep two tiers or three, I'm leaning toward dropping the middle "presets" tier entirely — just have presets-as-tools or raw React code — and for where that React runs, recommending the sandboxed iframe with our component kit as the simpler, fully-interactive option, while still flagging server-side rendering as a viable alternative worth considering.

Thinking further, presets are still worth keeping even if React can do everything, since they're faster, cheaper, and guaranteed quality as native-rendered tool calls like a stat card or bar list. And the custom-code path should work as a "skill" the agent loads on demand — a single tool whose instructions reveal the kit's API docs only when needed, following a progressive-disclosure pattern rather than bloating every tool description upfront.

For editing existing code, I need to map out what gets reused versus replaced: keeping artifact_versions, artifact_builds, ArtifactFrame, artifact-data, and dashboard layouts, but swapping the after()-based route builder for a workflow and removing the old widget path and fit logic. I also want to check how chat achieves durability — whether route.ts uses a workflow internally or some other resumable mechanism — since I didn't find explicit workflow calls when grepping the chat code.

content.thinking:
Chat durability relies on a persisted request row plus message history, so reopening the chat can find the running request, poll it, steer it, or cancel it. The artifact builder already has a similar build row and after() hook, but it's missing an equivalent message thread, cancellation support, and live progress on return — those are the gaps I need to close to match chat's durability pattern.

The cleanest fix is to reuse chat's conversation infrastructure directly: let an artifact thread just be a conversation with an attached artifact_id, and have the chat route inject artifact-specific tools (write_page, card presets, write_card_code) plus the current page/card context when that's set. That way durability, steering, cancellation, attachments, and voice all come for free, since the artifact agent is really just the chat agent with extra tools — though I'll need to bump maxDuration from 120s to something like 300s since HTML generation can run up to 280s.

I'm also considering making write_page a sub-agent call: the main chat agent gathers data and context, then invokes the artifact model with a brief to actually generate the HTML/React, keeping the designer model separate from the orchestrating chat model. On the tier question, I agree with dropping tier 2 and going straight to a React-code-generation tier for anything presets can't handle, including multi-chart support — still need to figure out where that generated React actually executes.

For presets, I'm thinking of exposing them as discrete tools like card_stat, card_bar_list, card_trend, etc., plus a card_custom tool that acts like write_page's sub-agent pattern: chat agent sends a brief plus queries, and the designer model writes the TSX using kit documentation baked into its instructions. This keeps card and page generation consistent, and editing requests just become new card_custom calls with an updated brief referencing the existing card.

On the technical side, I need to compile TSX to JS server-side on save (likely via sucrase or esbuild as a lightweight added dependency), then serve a kit bundle — React, our primitives, and the app's Tailwind CSS — as a static asset within the sandboxed iframe. I'm working through whether CSP's 'self' directive still resolves correctly against the app's origin when the document is sandboxed with an opaque origin, since that affects how script-src restrictions apply.

For visual consistency, presets still render natively server-side rather than in an iframe, but both presets and sandboxed tier-3 cards draw from the same shared component library, so the native look stays guaranteed either way. For interactivity, tier 3 cards keep local React state within the iframe, request new data via postMessage to the parent (which fetches from the cards API and relays it back), and handle navigation by postMessaging a target path that the parent validates against an allowlist before routing. I'm also settling on fixed-size slots for these iframes to keep layout predictable.

Since there's no headless browser check in production, overflow handling relies on kit components being size-aware (clipping lists with a "+N more" indicator) and the preview reporting overflow back so the user can notice and ask for adjustments. I'm also starting to lay out which existing pieces to reuse versus change — starting with extending conversations and chat_requests plus the /api/chat endpoint to support artifact-based chats by adding an artifact_id column.

Continuing the reuse/edit list: artifacts and artifact_versions stay with possible conversation links; artifact-data.ts gets its source registry replaced with one shared across chat tools so saved queries can reference any read tool; the frame route and ArtifactFrame get extended to support card frames while dropping the old widget-view/fit params; dashboard_layouts items get a schema shape change via code-only migration rather than rewriting applied ones; setArtifactOnHome becomes setCardOnHome(cardId, size); and the artifact viewer page needs its aside versions list replaced.

I'm now planning the new pieces needed: a versioned `artifact_cards` table holding kind, spec/code, queries, params, and sizes; a cards kit with preset renderers; a `/api/cards/[id]` route plus card frame route; and designer sub-agents for pages and cards. On the removal side, I need to drop the old artifact builder POST route, the builds table and its polling UI, the old artifact prompt component (replaced by chat input reuse), the widget view instructions, and fit sizing, while keeping ArtifactThumbnail for the gallery.

Now I want to check whether there's an existing chat UI component I can reuse for this, likely somewhere under the AI app folder, so I'll look for its name.

content.text:
## Yes: render the AI's React on our server, not in the browser

AI-written card code gets the freedom of Tier 3 and the speed and native look of Tiers 1–2. It runs **once on the server inside a real sandbox**. The browser only receives a safe element tree, which our own React draws directly in the Home grid. There is no iframe, and no AI JavaScript ever runs in the browser.

| | Sandboxed iframe (earlier plan) | **Server-rendered sandbox (new)** |
|---|---|---|
| Speed on Home | An extra request per card, plus a skeleton, plus loading charts from a CDN | Same as built-in cards: rendered with the page, cached |
| Looks native | Close, because we load our kit into it | **Identical**: it's real DOM inside our grid with our fonts and theme, and dark mode needs no reload |
| Freedom | Full | Full JSX, multiple charts, free layout, custom SVG, scoped CSS and animations |
| Safety | Good (isolated origin) | Stronger: the AI's code never runs in the browser |
| Can't do | — | Arbitrary client JavaScript such as canvas animation or live slider maths. Those are rare on Home; see the last decision below. |

## How it works

1. The card agent writes `card.tsx`: a pure function `Card({ data, params, size })`. It can use plain HTML, SVG and our kit components (`<Kit.BarList>`, `<Kit.Chart option={…}>`, `<Kit.Tabs>`, `<Kit.Segmented>`, `<Kit.Link>`, `<Kit.Tooltip>`…).
2. **When saved**, esbuild compiles it to plain JS. esbuild is already in `node_modules`.
3. **When rendered**, the code runs in **QuickJS (WASM)**, which is also already in `node_modules`. The sandbox has no network, filesystem, environment variables or clock, with limits of about 50 ms and 32 MB. Its input is only that card's query results. Its output is a JSON tree such as `{type:"div", props, children}`.
4. **On the host**, the tree is checked against an allowlist. Our server React then renders it: kit nodes become our real components, and text is escaped by React. Charts run through our own ECharts (v6, already a dependency), so the AI gets full ECharts styling but passes only option *data* and no functions.
5. Results are **cached** by card version, params and a hash of the data. Home pays for the sandbox only when the data has changed, and even then it costs tens of milliseconds per card, with cards rendered in parallel.

**Interactivity:**
- Interactive pieces are **our** client components: tabs, toggles, tooltips, hover, and drill-through links checked against an allowlist of app routes.
- Tabs render every panel up front and switch instantly.
- Changing a param (month, period, account) re-runs that card's queries plus the sandbox on the server, about 100 ms.

## Safety layers

1. **Code:** it runs only in QuickJS on the server, under time and memory limits, with no outside access.
2. **Data:** the card sees only its saved queries, which respect your AI data scopes.
3. **Output:**
   - an allowlist of HTML and SVG elements and attributes, with no `script`, `on*`, `iframe` or `foreignObject`
   - a limit on the number of nodes
   - links only to app routes
   - images only as `data:`
4. **CSS:**
   - `lightningcss` (already present) scopes every selector and `@keyframes` to the card and strips `url()` and `@import`
   - inline styles go through a property allowlist
   - `position: fixed` is not allowed

## Artistic freedom

- The card designer gets our kit and design tokens as defaults, but can ignore them when you ask for a specific look: gradients, illustrations drawn in SVG, custom typography using our font stack, animated rings, several charts in one card.
- The size (S/M/L/XL) is passed in as a prop, so one card can lay itself out differently at each size.

## Final plan, with your last message folded in

**The agent is the chat itself:**
- An artifact gets its own conversation, which runs through `/api/chat` with the artifact tools added.
- So it has **all chat tools** plus chat's durability: the `chat_requests` row, `after()`, resuming when you reopen, cancel, steer, the mic and attachments.
- Saved queries can use any read tool.

**Artifact tools:**
- `write_page(brief, queries)` and `write_card_code(brief, queries, params, sizes)` hand off to the designer model and include the current version when editing.
- The 6 presets are tools (`card_stat`, `card_bar_list`, …). They are pre-written `card.tsx` files in our repo and run natively with no sandbox.
- The agent uses a preset if one fits. Otherwise it uses the card-code skill, which is the default for anything with several parts or charts.

**Edit, don't duplicate:**

| Edit | New | Remove |
|---|---|---|
| `conversations` gets `artifact_id`; chat route gets artifact tools; `maxDuration` → 300 | `artifact_cards` (versioned: preset or code, compiled JS, queries, params, sizes) | `POST /api/artifacts` builder and `artifact_builds` with its builds UI and polling |
| `artifact-data.ts` → shared read-tool registry taken from the chat tools | `lib/cards/` (kit, QuickJS runner, sanitizer, renderer) | `MONEO_VIEW` widget path, `fit` sizing, `artifact-prompt.tsx` (replaced by the chat input) |
| Artifact viewer → chat panel with Page and Home card tabs | `GET /api/cards/[id]?params` | Mercury design prompt in the examples |
| `dashboard_layouts.items` → `{key, size}`; `setArtifactOnHome` → `setCardOnHome(card, size)` | | |
| Page frame route and `ArtifactFrame` stay for the full Page | | |

**About chat's durability:** it also dies on a deploy or crash mid-run, because it's `after()`-based. Artifacts will match chat exactly. Moving both to Workflow is a separate, later upgrade.

## Last decisions

1. **Cards that need live client JavaScript** (e.g. a what-if slider computed in the browser): skip them on Home, or allow a rare sandboxed "live card" iframe fallback? I'd skip them for now. A slider can trigger a server re-render with a short delay, and that's fast enough.
2. **Draft vs publish:** chat edits to a pinned card stay as drafts until you press "Update on Home"? I'd say yes.
3. **Several cards per artifact:** yes?

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

**Do not spawn agents unless the user asks.** Each spawn starts cold and re-derives context you already have — it's the expensive path on this plan. A task with "multiple angles," "thorough," or several parts is not a request to spawn; handle it inline with your own tools. Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

run_in_background.description: Agents run in the background by default; you will be notified when one completes. Set to false only when your very next action depends on this agent's result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise leave it in the background so the user can hand you other work.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

This tool runs Git Bash (POSIX sh), not cmd.exe or PowerShell. Use Unix shell syntax: `/dev/null` not `NUL`, forward slashes, `$VAR` not `%VAR%` or `$env:VAR`. Do not use PowerShell here-strings (`@'…'@`) or backtick continuation here — for multi-line strings use a heredoc.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. With it, `timeout` is how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000, max 7200000); at that limit it is stopped and you are re-invoked. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description: Fast file pattern matching. Supports glob patterns like "**/*.js" or "src/**/*.ts". Returns matching file paths sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: The glob pattern to match files against

path.description: The directory to search in. If not specified, the current working directory will be used. IMPORTANT: Omit this field to use the default directory. DO NOT enter "undefined" or "null" - simply omit it for the default behavior. Must be a valid directory path if provided.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Content search built on ripgrep. Prefer this over `grep`/`rg` via Bash — results integrate with the permission UI and file links.

- Full regex syntax (e.g. "log.*Error", "function\s+\w+"). Ripgrep, not grep — escape literal braces (`interface\{\}`).
- Filter with `glob` (e.g. "**/*.tsx") or `type` (e.g. "js", "py", "rust").
- `output_mode`: "content" (matching lines), "files_with_matches" (paths only, default), or "count".
- `multiline: true` for patterns that span lines.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes. With `run_in_background` the timeout is instead how long the command may run in the background (default 1800000ms / 30 minutes, max 7200000ms / 2 hours); at that limit it is stopped and you are notified.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice.

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background. With it, `timeout` limits how long the command may run in the background before it is stopped (default 1800000 ms, max 7200000 ms).

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

level.description: Effort level the review ran at

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

verdict.description: Set when a verify pass ran; absent on inline-only reviews

outcome.description: Set ONLY when re-reporting after applying fixes: what happened to this finding

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

input.title: Review artifact Home-card architecture plan
input.task:
You are reviewing an architecture PLAN (no code yet) for the Moneo repo in your working directory (Next.js 16 + React 19 + TS personal-finance app, Supabase/Postgres, Vercel AI SDK, Vercel Workflow). Read AGENTS.md first. Do NOT edit any files and do not commit; this is a read-only review. Read the code as needed to verify claims.

Goal: tell us whether this plan is right for our needs, and find (1) loopholes/bugs in the design, (2) security problems, (3) simpler ways to get the same result, (4) better ways. Be concrete: cite files/lines, give a failure scenario for each problem, and a proposed fix. Rank findings by severity. If a part of the plan is good, say so in one line; don't pad. The app currently has one user (the developer), so backward compatibility / migrating old artifacts is NOT a constraint.

## Context: what exists today (verify)
- Artifacts = AI-built interactive HTML pages over the user's finance data. Builder: `app/api/artifacts/route.ts` (generateText + tools from `ARTIFACT_SOURCES` in `lib/ai/artifact-data.ts`, save_artifact tool, runs in `after()`, status in `artifact_builds` table). Page renders in a sandboxed iframe from `app/ai/artifacts/[id]/frame/route.ts` with a strict CSP (`ARTIFACT_FRAME_CSP`), data injected as `window.MONEO_DATA` from saved read-only queries that re-run on each open (dates roll forward).
- "Add to Home" (`app/dashboard-actions.ts` setArtifactOnHome, `lib/finance/dashboard.ts`, `app/page.tsx`) pins the same HTML as an iframe in `view=widget` mode (`components/artifact-frame.tsx`, `fit` auto-height 160–560px). The user is unhappy: widget is an afterthought of one HTML doing two views, heights vary/scroll, no preview before pinning, iframe per card is slow and not native-looking.
- Artifact data sources are a subset of chat's read tools (chat in `app/api/chat/route.ts` also has finance_detail, finance_entities, finance_scenario, forecast_evaluate, wealth_list, agents_findings, etc.).
- Chat durability: `chat_requests` row (running/completed/failed/canceled), `after()` keeps the run alive when the tab closes, reopening a conversation finds the running request; steer/cancel exist. Not Workflow-based.

## The plan to review
1. **Agent = the chat itself.** Each artifact gets its own conversation (`conversations.artifact_id`), running through `/api/chat` with extra artifact tools, so it has ALL chat tools and chat's durability (chat_requests, after(), resume on reopen, cancel, steer, mic, attachments). Raise chat `maxDuration` to 300. Saved artifact/card queries can reference any read tool via a shared read-only tool registry extracted from chat tools (replacing `ARTIFACT_SOURCES`), and re-run on each view with roll-forward dates.
2. **Artifact tools:** `write_page(brief, queries)` and `write_card_code(brief, queries, params, sizes)` delegate to a designer model (settings `ai_models.artifacts`), given the current version when editing. Six preset card tools (`card_stat`, `card_stat_row`, `card_bar_list`, `card_trend`, `card_progress`, `card_list`) = pre-written trusted card components in our repo, filled with data bindings; agent uses a preset if it fits, else the card-code "skill" (default for multi-part / multi-chart cards). The full Page stays sandboxed-iframe HTML, with an injected Moneo CSS kit as default design (user-requested styles override).
3. **Home cards from AI code, rendered server-side, no iframe:**
   - Designer writes `card.tsx`: pure function `Card({ data, params, size })` using plain HTML, SVG and kit components (`Kit.BarList`, `Kit.Chart option={...}`, `Kit.Tabs`, `Kit.Segmented`, `Kit.Link`, `Kit.Tooltip`, ...). No hooks/effects.
   - On save, compile with esbuild. On render, run in QuickJS (quickjs-emscripten, WASM) with no network/fs/env/clock, ~50ms / 32MB limits; input = only that card's query results; output = a JSON element tree `{type, props, children}`.
   - Host validates the tree against an allowlist (HTML+SVG elements/attrs; no script, on*, iframe, foreignObject; node cap; links only to allowlisted app routes; images only data:), maps kit nodes to our real React components (client components for tabs/tooltips/hover/drill links), renders with React (text auto-escaped). Charts: AI passes ECharts option DATA only (no functions), rendered by our own ECharts (v6, already a dep).
   - CSS: lightningcss scopes selectors and @keyframes to the card, strips url()/@import; inline styles via a property allowlist; no position:fixed.
   - Cache rendered tree keyed by (card version, params, data hash).
   - Interactivity: tabs pre-render all panels and switch client-side; params (month/period/account) declared with allowed values -> `GET /api/cards/[id]?params` re-runs that card's queries + sandbox (~100ms). No arbitrary client JS on Home (no live-slider maths in browser); sliders debounce a server re-render.
4. **UX:** artifact page = chat panel + tabs "Page" / "Home card". Home card tab previews the card inside the real Home grid component with real neighbours and live data, size chips S/M/L/XL (fixed grid slots 2/3/4/6 cols, fixed height, no scroll; size passed as prop). Chat edits to a pinned card create a draft; "Update on Home" publishes a specific card version. Several cards per artifact allowed.
5. **Data model:** keep `artifacts`, `artifact_versions` (page). New versioned `artifact_cards` (artifact_id, version, kind preset|code, source tsx, compiled js, queries, params, sizes, published flag/version). `dashboard_layouts.items` becomes `{key, size}`. Remove: `POST /api/artifacts` builder, `artifact_builds` + builds UI/polling, `MONEO_VIEW` widget path, `fit` sizing, `artifact-prompt.tsx`, Mercury design prompt in `lib/ai/artifact-examples.ts`.

## Specifically check
- Security of running AI-written code in QuickJS on the server inside a Next.js route (escape risk, DoS, memory, prompt-injection from transaction text into the code or tree, tree/prop injection into our kit components, CSS exfiltration/overlay/clickjacking within the Home page, link/redirect abuse, ECharts option fields that accept HTML strings or functions like tooltip.formatter/rich text, SVG attack surface like <use href>, <animate> attribute tricks, xlink:href, style injection).
- Whether "agent = chat route" is actually a good fit (chat maxDuration, model choice, tool count/prompt bloat, long HTML generation inside a chat turn, how a designer sub-call reports progress, cancellation mid designer call).
- Whether saved queries over ALL read tools is safe/stable (scopes, tools that need entity ids, pagination cursors, tools whose output includes evidence links, cost/latency on Home with N cards).
- Caching correctness (data hash, per-user isolation, theme, params) and Home load performance.
- Is QuickJS actually needed vs a simpler approach (e.g. AI emits the JSON tree directly / JSX string parsed without execution / a constrained template language)? Compare honestly on freedom, speed, safety, complexity.
- Anything in the draft/publish, versioning, or layout `{key,size}` design that breaks.

Output: a ranked findings list (severity, problem, failure scenario, fix), then a short "simpler/better alternatives" section, then a verdict (adopt as-is / adopt with changes / rethink) in one paragraph. Keep it tight.

Delegated task node:delegated-task:command%3Amcp%3Aeb801510-d879-4c5f-a2ce-741f41c223ae%3Adelegate-task%3A06f357c5-c217-4950-a1e3-ed345f305bf8 (Review artifact Home-card architecture plan) [completed]:
**Adopt with changes.** Separating Page from Home cards, using trusted presets, previewing in the real grid, and publishing explicit versions are good decisions. The weakest part is introducing a general code runtime and broad rendering surface before defining their security contracts.

Ranked findings follow. References identify existing behavior; proposed components have no code yet.

1. **High — “JSON only” does not make kit props or ECharts safe.**  
   Existing artifacts have an opaque-origin sandbox ([artifact-data.ts:97](lib/ai/artifact-data.ts:97)); native cards lose that boundary. A transaction description could prompt the designer to emit malicious chart options, which bypass HTML-element validation through `Kit.Chart`. ECharts explicitly documents raw HTML in `tooltip.formatter` and URL handling in `title.link`; banning functions is insufficient. [Official security guidance](https://echarts.apache.org/handbook/en/best-practices/security/).  
   **Fix:** strict schemas per kit component, rejecting unknown props. Prefer a small chart specification compiled into options by trusted code. Own tooltip rendering, links, images, toolbox actions, and event handlers. Never spread arbitrary props into React components; reject `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `srcDoc`, executable URLs, and prototype-related keys recursively.

2. **High — CSS scoping is not containment.**  
   Today’s frame cannot style Home; the proposed native card can. Scoped descendants with absolute positioning, extreme dimensions, negative margins, transforms or high stacking order can cover neighbours. SVG references/animation and URL-bearing presentation attributes create additional paths outside a simple `on*` filter.  
   **Scenario:** a generated “account verification” overlay captures clicks over the real dashboard.  
   **Fix:** trusted positioned, clipped, isolated card wrappers; bounded dimensions and stacking; curated style tokens instead of arbitrary CSS initially. Use a minimal SVG subset, excluding animation, `use`, external references and arbitrary `style`; namespace permitted IDs. Restrict data images by MIME type and byte size, preferably to raster formats. Build links from typed route IDs and owned entity IDs; do not accept arbitrary URLs merely because their pathname looks internal.

3. **High — QuickJS limits do not bound the whole request.**  
   Compilation, input serialization, output extraction, validation and chart rendering happen outside the proposed 50ms execution budget. Large inputs or output strings can exhaust host memory before the node cap is checked. Concurrent cards multiply this cost. QuickJS provides runtime memory, stack and interrupt controls, but those are distinct controls, not a total request budget. [Runtime documentation](https://github.com/justjake/quickjs-emscripten/blob/main/doc/quickjs-emscripten-core/classes/QuickJSRuntime.md).  
   **Fix:** if retaining execution, use a killable worker/process with bounded concurrency and total deadlines; cap source, input/output bytes, depth, strings, chart points and compilation resources. Disable imports and all host capabilities; use an explicit JSX-to-tree runtime, never execute generated modules in Node. Benchmark WASM cold starts before promising ~100ms.

4. **High — Reusable read tools need a narrower contract than chat tools.**  
   Existing saved queries validate inputs, enforce scopes and strip internal evidence ([artifact-data.ts:36–53](lib/ai/artifact-data.ts:36)). Chat additionally refreshes authorization around execution ([chat route:155–166](app/api/chat/route.ts:155)). Extracting closures or exposing every nominally read tool risks losing these properties. “Read-only” also includes expensive scenarios and context-dependent detail/pagination results.  
   **Scenario:** a saved recurring-series cursor becomes stale, or a card repeatedly evaluates a costly scenario on every Home load.  
   **Fix:** share underlying read services, but require explicit `persistable` adapters with schemas, required scopes, owned-ID checks, output projection, cost limits and date/pagination semantics. Recheck scopes on every view, including cache hits. Keep evidence URLs out of generic link props.

5. **High — Arbitrary card computation can violate financial truth.**  
   The current prompt already delegates display maths to generated code ([artifact builder:26](app/api/artifacts/route.ts:26)); moving that code onto Home makes misleading totals more authoritative. A card can convert large minor-unit strings to `Number`, combine currencies, or hard-code an amount while still passing every sandbox check.  
   **Fix:** application queries produce authoritative totals, currency groups and scenario results. Bind financial values through trusted formatting components. Keep generated transformations to presentation; label hypothetical results explicitly. A sandbox prevents capabilities, not incorrect arithmetic or invented claims.

6. **Medium — Chat reuse is sensible; raising `maxDuration` alone does not provide the proposed lifecycle.**  
   Chat currently has a **90-second model timeout** ([chat route:227](app/api/chat/route.ts:227)); the artifact builder allows 280 seconds and 32,000 output tokens ([artifact builder:89–91](app/api/artifacts/route.ts:89)). Cancellation is noticed at boundaries ([chat route:87–91](app/api/chat/route.ts:87)), so a nested designer call could continue and save after cancellation. `after()` preserves execution after disconnect, but is not crash-restart durability.  
   **Fix:** pass one deadline/cancellation contract through parent and designer; check request status immediately before saving. Persist designer-stage progress for reopening, and make saves idempotent by request/tool-call ID. Keep generated source out of ordinary chat history; return a version reference. Enable artifact tools only in artifact conversations, and give the designer only its necessary data/schema. Use Workflow only if restart/resume across process loss is required.

7. **Medium — Generic date rolling breaks semantic periods.**  
   Current logic shifts every nested `from`/`to` by elapsed days ([artifact-data.ts:68–90](lib/ai/artifact-data.ts:68)). A “this month” card saved mid-month eventually displays a sliding interval rather than the current calendar month; historical comparisons may move unintentionally. Broader tools introduce more date meanings.  
   **Fix:** save explicit period expressions—current month, previous month, trailing days, fixed dates—and resolve them in the workspace timezone. Declare which fields accept parameter bindings; do not recursively rewrite arbitrary inputs.

8. **Medium — The cache misses the expensive work and omits render inputs.**  
   Computing a data hash requires fetching data first, so the proposed cache mostly saves sandbox execution. Existing queries fan out up to 12 calls per artifact ([artifact-data.ts:44](lib/ai/artifact-data.ts:44), [89](lib/ai/artifact-data.ts:89)); many cards can overwhelm Home. Omitting `size` gives incorrect trees after resizing.  
   **Fix:** batch/deduplicate normalized queries per workspace and render cards independently with bounded concurrency and failure states. Cache keys need card identity/version, workspace/user authorization context, normalized params, size, renderer version, and any consumed locale/timezone/theme settings. Keep HTTP responses private; use CSS variables for theme where possible. Treat latency targets as measurements to establish.

9. **Medium — Card identity and publication are underspecified.**  
   Current keys identify an artifact, allowing only one Home entry per artifact ([dashboard.ts:8–14](lib/finance/dashboard.ts:8)). A row containing both card versions and a `published` flag does not establish stable identity or atomic publication.  
   **Scenario:** editing one of several cards updates the wrong slot, or concurrent edits overwrite a newer draft/publication.  
   **Fix:** separate stable card IDs from immutable version rows; store one published-version pointer per card, updated transactionally with optimistic concurrency. Home keys identify cards; layout entries also need per-instance params if instances may differ. Preserve existing layout conflict checks ([dashboard-actions.ts:14–15](app/dashboard-actions.ts:14)). Scope conversation/card relationships to the workspace with RLS and constraints.

10. **Medium — Fixed heights need responsive and overflow rules.**  
    Existing layout validation accepts strings, with uniqueness and a 50-item limit ([dashboard.ts:11](lib/finance/dashboard.ts:11)). `{key,size}` requires coordinated database/schema/action/UI changes. Desktop spans of 2/3/4/6 alone do not define mobile behavior.  
    **Scenario:** long labels, zoom or larger fonts hide financial values and keyboard-focused controls in a clipped card.  
    **Fix:** define responsive spans, trusted content budgets, truncation rules and a reliable “Open page” action. Validate every supported size with realistic long/empty/error data; preview pinning against the exact published version.

**Simpler/better alternatives**

Start with a **versioned JSON card document**: trusted layout primitives, data bindings, bounded repetition/conditions, presets and a constrained chart schema. The AI writes this once; application code resolves bindings on each view. This supports multi-part cards without QuickJS, esbuild or a general CSS sanitizer.

Raw JSON trees alone cannot safely refresh hard-coded values; bindings are essential. Parsing JSX without execution still needs a constrained expression language for loops/calculations, so it mainly changes syntax. QuickJS offers substantially more computational freedom, but adds operational and security complexity that the stated Home requirements do not yet justify. Keep unrestricted interaction in the sandboxed Page and introduce executable cards only after a concrete limitation warrants them.

**Verdict:** adopt with changes: reuse chat orchestration, split Page/card versions, and implement explicit publication and native previews. Begin with declarative cards and curated persistable query adapters; defer QuickJS until the simpler renderer demonstrably cannot meet a real card requirement. This was a read-only architecture review; no files changed or tests run, and the proposed sandbox’s actual isolation and latency remain unverified.

content.thinking:
I need to summarize this review honestly for the user, flagging a real tension: the reviewer suggests declarative JSON over QuickJS, but the user already rejected that approach in favor of presets plus React code for creative freedom. Most other findings — chart options, CSS overlay, query adapters, financial accuracy, cancellation, date periods, card identity, cache keys — hold regardless of that choice, so I want to separate those from the QuickJS-vs-JSON debate and give my own view on it.

Given the user's priority on freedom, I'd lean toward keeping the code-based approach but hardening it: running QuickJS in a worker thread with hard kill limits and resource caps, treating money values as trusted pre-formatted tokens rather than raw computation, enforcing strict per-kit prop schemas and a constrained chart spec, and using CSS containment (`contain: paint`, overflow clip, isolation) so nothing can visually escape its card — which also neutralizes the overlay/position risks the reviewer raised.

Still, I'm weighing the alternative: a declarative JSON document with layout primitives, style tokens, and SVG primitives could offer nearly the same expressive freedom while being simpler and safer, since the AI only needs to author it once and the real risk (loops, conditionals, computed money) stays in code either way. The simplicity principle pushes me to question whether code execution is even necessary if financial values are bound through trusted components and the code's real job is just layout.

I'm going to reverse my earlier stance: recommend adopting the declarative document approach, but push for it to be expressive enough to handle free nesting, rich styling, multiple charts, and SVG shapes, so it doesn't feel like the constrained "6 templates" the user rejected — presets become just saved documents, with QuickJS kept as a later escape hatch. I want to directly address the user's earlier "why have 2" objection by clarifying this format can support multi-chart, freely laid-out designs, since it's really just the AI writing the whole card in JSON instead of JSX, then list the fixes I'm keeping regardless and ask for their decision concisely.

content.text:
The review's verdict is **adopt with changes**. It agrees with splitting Page from Home card, using the chat as the agent, previewing in the real Home grid, and publishing explicit versions. Its main point is that running AI-written code with QuickJS is the weakest part, and I think it's right.

## The big question: QuickJS vs a card document

Its argument is that the risk isn't really the code running; it's what the code outputs. Both approaches need the same safeguards, so QuickJS adds a runtime, esbuild, a CSS sanitizer and worker limits without solving the hard problems:

- **Chart settings can carry HTML and links.** ECharts accepts raw HTML in places like tooltip formatters and link fields, so even "data only, no functions" is open to injection. Every kit component needs a strict schema, and charts need our own small chart spec that trusted code turns into ECharts settings.
- **Card styles can cover the rest of Home.** Without an iframe, card CSS could draw a fake overlay over the real dashboard. Cards need a clipped, isolated wrapper plus a style allowlist.
- **Code can do money maths wrong.** It could combine currencies or lose precision with `Number`, and nothing in the sandbox would catch it. Totals have to come from app queries anyway, so the card code would only be doing layout.

If the code is only doing layout, the AI can write the same thing as a **JSON card document**:
- free nesting
- repeat over data
- shown/hidden when a list is empty
- multiple charts
- SVG shapes
- rich style tokens such as gradients and type sizes

**What it can't do is arbitrary calculation, which shouldn't live in a card anyway.** This is not "6 templates". The AI designs a whole card; it just writes it as data instead of JSX. The presets become saved documents.

**I'm changing my recommendation:** use the card document now, keep the full freedom of the Page in its iframe, and add QuickJS later only if a real card needs it. That's simpler and safer, and it's still native and fast.

## Fixes I'm taking regardless

- **Saved queries use explicit "persistable" adapters, not the raw chat tools.** Each adapter has a schema, scopes checked again on every view (including cache hits), checks that any ids belong to you, a cost limit, and no evidence links or pagination cursors.
- **Periods are saved as meaning, not shifted dates.** "Current month" or "last 90 days" is stored as that and resolved in your timezone. Today's code moves every date by the number of days elapsed, which turns "this month" into a sliding window.
- **The designer call shares the chat's deadline and cancel.** It checks status just before saving, saves only once per request, and progress is saved so a reopened tab sees it. Generated source stays out of the chat history (the chat only gets a version reference), and the artifact tools exist only in artifact conversations. One correction from the review: chat's model timeout is 90s, so raising `maxDuration` alone isn't enough.
- **Cards have stable ids, separate from immutable version rows.** Each card has one published-version pointer, updated with conflict checks. Home layout keys point to cards, not artifacts.
- **Home loads cheaply.** Repeated queries across cards are combined, cards render independently with a cap on how many run at once, and each card has its own error state. The cache key includes size, workspace, renderer version and timezone. Theme uses CSS variables, so the cache doesn't need it.
- **Fixed sizes come with rules.** Mobile column spans, limits on how much content each size holds, truncation, an "Open" link that's always visible, and preview tests with long, empty and error data.

## Your call

1. **Card document now, QuickJS only if needed later** (my recommendation, and the reviewer's), or **QuickJS code now with all the hardening above**?
