content.text:
The design below follows the reviewer's recommendation. Nothing is built yet.

## For you

- **One chat per artifact.** Every artifact is a conversation using the same chat, so it has all of chat's tools, the mic and attachments. It keeps running if you leave or close the site, and you find it in progress when you come back. You can cancel or steer it mid-build.
- **Two outputs, side by side:**
  - **Page:** the full interactive HTML (sliders, what-ifs). It uses our Moneo design kit by default and follows any style you ask for.
  - **Home card:** a compact native card.
- **Adding to Home:**
  1. You say "add to Home" or press the button.
  2. The **Home card** tab shows the card inside your real Home, next to your real cards, with live data.
  3. You pick a size: S, M, L or XL. Sizes have a fixed height and never scroll.
  4. You refine it in the same chat, e.g. "also show the yearly total" or "drop the chart".
  5. You press **Add to Home**.
- **Editing later:** chat changes to a card that's already on Home stay as a draft until you press **Update on Home**, so Home never changes without you seeing it first. Every version is kept and can be undone.
- **On Home:** cards look and load like Net worth or Briefing: no iframe and no skeleton flash, and dark mode just works. They're clickable: month or period switches, tabs, tooltips, and bars that open Transactions. One artifact can have several cards.

## How it works

- **Agent:** the chat route with artifact-only tools:
  - `write_page`: the designer model writes the HTML
  - `write_card`: the designer writes a card document
  - 6 preset card tools for common shapes
- **Card document:** JSON the AI designs freely: nested layout, repeated rows, multiple charts, SVG shapes, style tokens. Our server renders it with our own React components. No AI code ever runs.
- **Data:** each card and page saves queries through "persistable" read adapters that cover every chat read tool. Scopes are checked on every view, and periods are stored as meaning ("this month"), not as fixed dates. All money totals come from app code; cards only display them.
- **Safety:**
  - every component prop is checked against a strict schema
  - charts use our own chart spec, so no raw ECharts HTML or links
  - each card sits in a clipped, isolated box and can't draw over Home
  - links can only go to app routes
  - the Page keeps its sandboxed iframe
- **Speed:** queries repeated across cards run once, cards render in parallel and each has its own error state, and renders are cached by card version, size and data.

## Code changes

| Edit | Add | Remove |
|---|---|---|
| Chat (artifact conversations and tools), artifact viewer (chat plus Page and Home card tabs), artifact data (adapters and period meaning), Home layout (`{card, size}`), frame route (Page only) | `artifact_cards` and card version tables with a published pointer, `lib/cards/` (document schema, renderer, kit), card data route | Old builder route, `artifact_builds` and its polling, widget mode in the HTML, auto-height iframes, old prompt box, Mercury design prompt |

**Later, only if needed:** AI-written React code in a sandbox, for card designs the document format can't express.

Say go and I'll build it in phases, with a commit per step.

content.text:
Agreed. Custom cards will be AI-written React, built with every safeguard the reviewer asked for. (The `write_card` document was meant as the "make its own" path, but React gives you more visual freedom.)

## How a card gets made

1. If one of the **6 presets** fits, the agent uses it. Presets are our own trusted code.
2. If none fits, the designer **writes its own React card** (`card.tsx`):
   - any layout, several charts, custom SVG art, its own styling and animations
   - a different layout for each size (S/M/L/XL)
   - the default for anything visual or with several parts

## How AI React runs safely and fast

- **Where it runs:** esbuild compiles it when saved. It then runs on the server in **QuickJS inside a worker that can be killed**:
  - no network, filesystem, environment variables, clock or imports
  - a hard total deadline
  - caps on code size, input and output size, tree depth and number of chart points
  - a limit on how many cards render at once
- **What it outputs:** an element tree, never HTML and never browser JavaScript. Our React renders it natively, so there's no iframe.
- **Checking the output:**
  - only allowed HTML and a safe subset of SVG (no `<use>`, animation tags, external references, `on*` or `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`)
  - images only as small `data:` rasters
  - every kit component has a strict prop schema that rejects anything unknown
- **Charts:** the card describes them with our own chart spec, and trusted code turns that into ECharts. No raw ECharts settings, so no HTML formatters or links get through.
- **Containment:** each card sits in an isolated, clipped wrapper (`contain: paint`, `overflow: clip`). Even absolutely positioned or animated content can't cover the rest of Home. Its CSS is scoped to the card, with `url()` and `@import` stripped.
- **Money:** the card can arrange and style figures but never computes them. Totals come from app queries and are shown through our `Kit.Money` component, and what-if values are labelled as estimates.
- **Links:** the card picks from typed app routes and your own ids, never free URLs.
- **Interactivity:** our own components handle tabs, toggles, tooltips and drill-through clicks. Changing a param re-renders that card on the server.
- **Cache:** results are cached by card version, size, params, data, timezone and renderer version. The sandbox runs only when something changes.

Everything else in the summary stays the same: chat as the durable agent with all tools, Page and Home card tabs, live preview in your real Home, drafts until "Update on Home", several cards per artifact, versioning and undo, and the code changes listed.

One honest caveat: QuickJS speed is a guess until I benchmark it. I'll measure that first. If it's too slow, I'll keep the same design and switch the engine.

Say go and I'll build it in phases, with a commit per step.

content.thinking:
This is a large, complex route, so I need to plan carefully but keep the implementation minimal yet real. I'm scoping out the work in phases: first benchmarking QuickJS and checking whether quickjs-emscripten is already a dependency, then building the card runtime library with presets and primitives as React server components like Money, Stat, BarList, and Chart.

I'm sketching out the sandbox runner that compiles tsx with esbuild and runs it inside QuickJS using a minimal tree-builder, plus a sanitizer that validates the resulting tree against allowed tags, attributes, and scoped styles, a renderer that maps the tree to React elements, and a Zod spec for the card record itself.

For the database layer I'm working through a migration introducing artifact_cards with stable IDs, versioned records, and a published version pointer, while removing the old artifact_builds table and linking conversations to artifacts. I'm also debating how dashboard layout items should encode size — whether to keep them as plain strings and add a separate size map, or simplify by storing size directly on the card record itself, which seems like the cleaner approach since each card only occupies one Home slot.

For chat integration, I'm reasoning through adding artifact-specific tools (write_page, card_preset, write_card_code) that activate when a conversation has an artifact_id, along with extended timeouts, a designer sub-call for generating updated HTML/TSX, progress events, and cancellation support via a stop signal. I'm also considering whether these tools need to be wrapped for progress display and sketching out a shared registry of persistable data adapters spanning entities, scenarios, wealth, and forecast sources.

Then I'm working out date handling — instead of shifting days, I want to support token-based date expressions like month boundaries, relative day counts, and prior period markers that get resolved into concrete dates within a timezone, replacing the old day-rolling logic entirely since it's cleaner and removes the need for pagination cursor handling.

For month-based parameters, I'm having cards declare params with a kind and default, plus token references that expand to start/end dates for that param.

Now I'm moving to the viewer UI phase, thinking through how the artifact page should reuse the existing chat panel components and hook, and planning out tabs for the page versus home card views with a mini preview grid.

Rendering real neighbor widgets inside the artifact page preview is too heavy, so the compromise is to render the actual card natively at its real slot width while ghosting neighboring cards as skeletons with real titles — giving an honest sense of how it'll look on the overview page. Then size chips feed a server action to set card size on the draft, with "Add to Home" and "Update on Home" triggering a publish action, and for the home page itself I'm planning to render each card by its id, loading the published version, running its queries, and rendering through the sandbox.

For param interactivity, I want a client wrapper that fetches the rendered tree JSON from an API route and renders it through the same isomorphic renderer — meaning the renderer and kit components need to be client-safe with no server-only dependencies, so the tree can be rendered identically on both server and client.

For phase 7, I'm planning to strip out the old builder route, artifact builds table, builds UI, prompt flow, widget mode, fit logic, and example design prompts, and rework the "New artifact" flow so it creates an artifact row plus a conversation together before sending the first message.

Then I need to wire the chat's suggest_artifact tool to link into the new artifact creation flow with a prompt param, write up the architecture docs page, and finish with tests, lint, build, and PR — which means I still need to dig into the chat client hook, the AI page, conversations schema, artifacts list page, prompt component, actions, route tests, the home page card code, dashboard settings layout, and package dependencies.

content.thinking:
Now I'm setting up the sandbox runtime file, importing QuickJS WASM module utilities and sucrase for transforming code before execution, and lazily initializing the module instance.

I'm defining a compileCard function that transpiles TypeScript/JSX source using sucrase with the custom h/Fragment pragma, blocking require calls, and exposing Kit as a global proxy whose properties resolve to string identifiers like "kit:BarList". I'm also writing the QuickJS prelude that defines h, Fragment, and a children-flattening helper that drops nullish/boolean values and stringifies numbers, then wrapping execution with CommonJS-style exports/module objects to extract the default export as the Card component.

For safety I'm keeping a deadline-based interrupt handler (around 1s) and a memory limit (64MB) even though output size and concurrency caps are being removed per the user's request, and considering whether to allow Date (useful for card formatting, though it complicates caching determinism). I'm planning to spin up a fresh runtime and context per render for workspace isolation, then move to building a recursive tree sanitizer that validates node types against an allowlist of HTML and SVG tags.

Now I'm defining the attribute allowlist for sanitized nodes, covering common HTML attributes plus a wide set of SVG geometry and styling attributes, and working out rules for safely allowing internal `url(#id)` references by namespacing IDs to the card instance to prevent collisions or external references.

I'm also restricting style objects to a curated allowlist of layout, typography, and color CSS properties, while being careful to only permit gradient-based background images rather than arbitrary URLs.

For scoping custom CSS per card, I'm weighing whether to allow a style block with keyframes, using CSS nesting to scope rules under a data-card attribute selector, though I'm unsure if keyframes can be nested that way—so I might need lightningcss with a visitor to handle scoping properly instead.

Actually, CSS modules with the pure option seems cleaner: it auto-renames classes and keyframes to unique hashed names and errors on non-local selectors, which solves scoping and prevents global leakage, while a visitor can separately reject disallowed url() usage and @import statements.

That confirms the real exfiltration risk — financial data leaking through URLs — so I need to block url() everywhere except url(#id), and note CSP could add another layer of defense. Fake phishing-style text inside a card is a minor injection concern worth noting but acceptable since it's user-requested content. For links, I need to figure out how Kit.Link's typed route params map to the actual query params supported by /money/transactions, which I'll check later.

For Kit components, Kit.Money needs to format values through the app's money formatter, but since a card could pass a literal value instead of trusted data, I can't fully guarantee provenance — I'll rely on prompt rules plus Kit.Money's formatting and existing `*_formatted` strings as a partial safeguard. For charts, I'm weighing whether to use echarts or write my own lightweight SVG chart renderer, leaning toward SSR-friendly custom SVG charts to avoid bloating the client bundle.

I also need to sketch out other Kit primitives: Tabs (requiring recursive validation since content is a prop tree), Segmented (client-side, tied to card instance context for refetching on param change), Link, Style, and possibly Progress, while treating Sparkline as covered by the Chart component.

For icons, dynamically importing all of lucide-react seems too heavy, so I'll skip that for now and keep the kit small.

Now I'm thinking through how presets should work — whether they're pre-written React components bound to data, or whether they should unify with the same tree-rendering pipeline as everything else, which feels like the simpler path.

If presets are just trusted TSX templates taking config as props, I could run them through the same QuickJS pipeline as native renderers, making for a single render path instead of maintaining separate native renderers. The tradeoff is performance, but if QuickJS is fast enough I should just benchmark it first and decide whether to unify.

For data binding, I'm imagining configs like specifying a title and a value path, with the template reading from the data object using that path. For params, I'm sketching out how cards would declare parameters with a name, kind, options, and default, and how queries would reference those params using token placeholders in the input strings.

Now I'm working out the token resolution system: handling tokens like today, days-ago offsets, month/year/week start and end (with offset support for previous periods), and param-based tokens that substitute values for month, period, or choice-kind parameters, validated against their declared options. I'm also thinking through saved queries as a list referencing shared sources and adapters.

For the artifact source registry, I'm deciding it should cover all the read-oriented tools—investigate, cashflow, transactions, balances, accounts, recurring, goals, entities, detail, scenario, wealth, forecast, agent findings—while excluding write-type actions like review/start or proposals, since those aren't meant to be queried as data sources.

Thinking about duplication between chat's inline tool definitions and the artifact-data registry, I'm deciding to keep chat's tools as-is since their descriptions carry chat-specific evidence semantics, but have the registry wire into the same underlying functions rather than duplicating logic. Now I'm working through how the chat route should detect an active artifact_id on the conversation and conditionally add tools like write_page, card_preset, and write_card when one exists.

I'm also planning the system prompt additions (current page metadata and card listings), extending timeouts for artifact conversations, and designing the write_page flow where queries run first to give the designer model real sample data before generating raw HTML output via a tool-free generateText call.

I'm thinking through the save step—checking cancellation status before inserting artifact_versions—and deciding to skip a formal idempotency column since each tool call only fires once. For the new-artifact flow, I'm mapping out how a user prompt on /ai/artifacts creates a blank artifact and conversation, redirects with the prompt as a query param, and shows an empty state until the first version is generated.

I'm also planning that writing a page updates both the artifact's title and the conversation title. For card tools, I'm sketching `card_preset` and `write_card`, where the designer generates TSX using kit docs and sample query data, compiles and test-renders it at all sizes with real data, and loops back to the designer up to twice if validation fails before saving a new draft version—backed by artifact_cards and artifact_card_versions tables.

Size is a user choice on the card itself rather than versioned, defaulting to "M," and changing it updates artifact_cards.size directly so pinned cards resize immediately on Home—treating it like a layout choice rather than something gated by draft/publish. The publish flow uses a published_version pointer so Home only ever shows the published version.

Adding a card to Home sets published_version and inserts its layout key, removing it nulls that pointer, and updating uses an optimistic check against the old version to avoid race conditions—Home filters to only show cards with a non-null published_version, and multiple cards per artifact are allowed. Rendering happens via a server component that loads the published version, runs its queries with resolved tokens, compiles to a tree through the sandbox, then hands off to a client CardView component that supports interactive param changes by refetching the tree from an API route.

For caching, I'm using an in-memory LRU keyed by a hash of compiled version, size, params, and data, scoped per workspace since version ids and data differ there—just a simple 200-entry map. To avoid redundant query execution across cards on the same Home render, I'll add a per-request memo object shared across all cards so identical queries aren't rerun. For previewing cards on the artifact page, I'm picturing a tab listing each card with its size chip and a live-rendered preview arranged in a grid that mimics the real Home layout, including ghost placeholders for neighboring cards.

Now I'm settling on fixed card dimensions: column spans of 2/3/4/6 for S/M/L/XL at the lg breakpoint, with a consistent height (around 300px) across all sizes, full-width on mobile. Each card wrapper clips overflow and isolates paint, with a header for title/open-link and a flexible body area whose width scales by size (roughly 360px for S up to 1100px for XL) while height stays fixed around 240px for the body.

I'm also planning design-kit additions — card, stat, eyebrow, grid, muted, and positive/negative classes — and updating the page designer instructions to drop the old view/fit options. I'm removing the ArtifactFrame's fit mode (keeping only thumbnail), since Home no longer depends on it, and tearing out the old artifact builds API, routes, and prompt components in favor of a simpler creation form.

For new artifact creation, I'm leaning toward a plain form that posts a prompt to a server action, redirects to the artifact page with the prompt in the URL, and lets the chat auto-send on mount if the conversation is empty — stripping the query param afterward so reloads don't resend it. On the data side, I'm dropping the artifact_builds table and adding a unique artifact_id foreign key to conversations.

I need to check schema.ts for how conversations and RLS are structured, look at the existing artifact and home-artifacts tests, and make sure artifact conversations get excluded from the main threads list by filtering on artifact_id being null in both loadThreads and search. The system prompt already points to /ai/artifacts?prompt= for suggesting artifacts, so the list page just needs to read that param to prefill — that part should be fine, as should the voice call panel since it reuses chat.

I also need to look at how the settings page handles the home layout, checking whether it shows built-in widgets alongside artifacts, and update the ARTIFACT_KEY reference in dashboard.ts to use the card key instead. Let me pull up those files along with the top of app/page.tsx, the artifact-home e2e test, and the home-artifacts test.

content.thinking:
Performance looks solid — roughly 1ms warm render, 44ms cold start, so QuickJS is fast enough and presets can share the same execution path. I should verify the output tree is correct with a quick print before moving on, then start designing the tree sanitizer module that will produce a safe node structure alongside the renderer.

For CSS scoping, lightningcss brings native binaries which complicates bundling/tracing on Vercel, so I'm leaning toward pure-JS postcss with manual selector prefixing instead: scoping each rule under a data-card attribute selector, renaming keyframes and rewriting their references, and rejecting risky at-rules and dangerous declaration values like url(), expression(), or behavior-related properties.

I also need to confirm unscoped CSS is genuinely risky — yes, an unscoped rule like `div { display:none }` could break the whole app, so scoping is non-negotiable.

Now I'm thinking through how the kit's SafeNode tree gets rendered: a client-safe `renderTree` function used inside a client CardView component so param changes can re-render with fresh trees from the API, while still getting SSR'd HTML for fast first paint. I'm also sketching the prop validation spec for kit components like Money, starting with fields like minor amount, currency code, signed, and compact flags.

Continuing that spec, I'm defining Chart's props (type, labels, series with colors, height, stacking, axis, value formatting) and validating that color tokens only allow safe CSS color syntax, plus specs for Tabs, Param, and Link components.

Now I'm thinking through how the client card context works — cardId, params, and option changes triggering a fetch to the card API endpoint that returns an updated tree — and how query data gets passed into the card as sample data for the designer. I'm deciding where to put the query resolution logic, leaning toward a dedicated artifact-data module under lib/ai.

I'm reworking the query resolution so it replaces date-rolling with a token-based resolver that takes today's date and params, and updating the artifact query runner to use this new approach consistently across both cards and saved artifact versions, dropping the old savedOn parameter entirely since backward compatibility isn't needed. Writing the params schema...

Now I'm defining how declared params get resolved against requested values and today's date into both a validated values map and date ranges for month/period types, plus computing display options server-side for the UI. I'm setting up token parsing for strings like "@paramName" or "@param:name.from" so queries can reference resolved param values, and confirming artifact pages only need query-level tokens since their interactivity lives client-side in the iframe.

Now I'm writing the database migration to drop the old artifact_builds table and link conversations to artifacts via a new foreign key column with a unique index. Writing migration SQL...

Finishing the schema fields, then I'm thinking through how preset cards generate their source from a template plus embedded config, keeping rendering unified between presets and code. I'm also working out cross-workspace integrity for artifact references, considering a composite foreign key tying artifact_id and workspace_id together via a unique constraint on artifacts to prevent referencing artifacts from another workspace.

Now I need to check how conversations get inserted for artifacts and whether the existing grants on conversations are column-scoped, so I should look at that migration for the grant style.
Benchmarks look solid: ~1 ms for a warm busy-card render, 44 ms on first render, and 7 ms for 8 cards at once, with presets able to reuse the same pipeline. Next I'll move on to schema and grants.

The plan I land on is navigating to the artifact page with a start query param, then having ArtifactChat forward that as an initialPrompt into a new autoSend prop on ChatForm, which fires sendMessage once on mount if there are no existing messages and guards against resending. I also want ChatForm to accept a separate selectionKey for artifact chats so it doesn't hijack the main conversation selection cookie, and I should adjust the empty-state suggestion text to be relevant to artifact creation rather than the generic money assistant prompt.

For the layout, I'm sketching a grid similar to the old design with a fixed-width sidebar and main content area. For the server-side actions, I'm planning a createArtifact action that inserts a new artifact row with a title derived from the prompt, creates an associated conversation, and redirects the client to the new artifact's page with the start param encoded so the chat auto-sends that initial prompt.

I also need deleteArtifact to properly filter from Home's card listing on soft delete, plus actions for setCardSize, publishCard (setting published_version and adding the card to the layout), and unpublishCard (removing it from the layout while keeping published_version). These all belong in the dashboard-actions file replacing the old setArtifactOnHome function.

For the shared dashboard utilities, I'm renaming the key helpers from artifact-based to card-based (CARD_KEY, cardWidgetKey, cardIdFromKey), and making the span calculation depend on a card size map instead.

On the Home page itself, I'm rewriting the pinned items logic to pull card ids from the layout, then query cards joined with their artifacts to filter out deleted artifacts and unpublished cards, rendering each inside a Suspense boundary with a skeleton fallback via an async HomeCard component.

HomeCard will load its version server-side and render through CardView, sharing one `shared` object created per request in Home. To keep things fast, I'll fetch each card's published version with small parallel per-card queries rather than one big filtered query, since Postgres can't easily filter matching id/version pairs together. I also need to update the settings page labels to reference cards instead of artifacts, and clean up the old ArtifactFrame component.

Keeping thumbnail loading state but dropping the fit code and FIT_* constants, and removing the `view` param from the frame route. Now I'm moving on to writing the ArtifactChat component.

Moneo · artifacts & Home cardsArchitectureA card's lifeRenderingSafetyDataDecisionsTested liveLimits

Moneo · personal finance · artifacts

Build it from your data, then live with it on Home.

An artifact is a page Moneo builds from your real finances, in its own chat. Any part of it can become a card on your Home: previewed in place, sized, published when you're happy, and drawn by the app itself — not an iframe. The model can design anything, but every number still comes from the app.

~1 msto run a busy card's code in the sandbox (warm)
0lines of AI code that run in your browser
1 chatbuilds the page and every card, with all chat tools
~1.5 sHome with a published card, production build

Architecture

One chat, two outputs, one data contract

The artifact's chat is the normal Moneo chat with four extra tools. A designer model writes the Page (HTML) or a card (React). The app saves the queries the work needs, never the numbers, and reruns them every time anything is shown.

A card's life

From “add this to Home” to a card you can trust

Every step is a normal chat request, so it keeps going if you close the tab and shows as working when you come back.

1 · ask

Say it in the chat

“Add a small card with last month's total and top categories, with a month switch.”

2 · read

The agent reads real data

It uses the same read tools as chat, then writes queries with dates as meaning (@param:month.from), never fixed dates.

3 · design

Preset or its own React

If one of six shapes fits, it fills a preset. Otherwise a designer writes the card's own TSX, with any layout, several charts or custom SVG.

4 · check

Rendered before it's saved

It's compiled and run at S, M, L and XL with live data, and the tree is checked. Failures go back to the designer up to 3 times.

5 · preview

A draft, in place

The Home cards tab shows it in its Home slot between your own widgets, live and interactive. Pick a size, then ask for changes.

6 · publish

You decide when Home changes

Add to Home publishes that exact version. Later edits are drafts until “Update on Home”, and every version is kept to go back to.

Rendering

AI-written React that never runs in your browser

The card's code runs once on the server inside QuickJS, a JavaScript engine compiled to WASM. Its only output is a tree of plain data, { type, props, children }. The app checks that tree and draws it with its own React, so it gets your fonts and theme, switches dark mode instantly, and has no iframe.

Measured (benchmark script in the repo)

9 mscompile TSX → JS (sucrase), once at save
44 msfirst render; the WASM engine starts
1.1 mswarm render p50 (p95 2.9 ms): two charts, 12 rows
7 ms8 cards at once

The cost on Home is the data queries, which every widget already pays. Cards on one Home share reads: the same query runs once.

What a card can use

HTML and SVG (gradients, filters, clip paths), style objects, and scoped CSS with :hover, @keyframes and @media. The kit, which the app draws:

Kit.MoneyKit.ChartKit.TabsKit.ParamKit.LinkKit.Style

Tabs switch instantly in the browser. A Param (month, period or choice) re-renders the card on the server with new data in about 100 ms. Links are built by the app from a typed target.

Safety

Five walls between the model and your Home

The model writes the code, and text in your transactions could try to steer it, so we treat both the code and its output as untrusted.

LayerWhat it stops
QuickJS sandboxfresh runtime per renderNo network, files, env, timers or imports. A 1 s deadline and a 64 MB memory ceiling stop a runaway loop from stalling Home; they aren't design limits.
Tree checkallowlistOnly known HTML/SVG elements and attributes get through: no script, iframe, img, a, use, foreignObject, event handlers or dangerouslySetInnerHTML. No url() except to the card's own namespaced ids, so data can't leave through a stylesheet.
Kit schemasstrict Zod per componentUnknown props are refused. Charts take numbers and labels only, never chart-library options that accept HTML or functions. Links take a typed page plus ids, never a URL.
Scoped CSSpostcssEvery selector is prefixed with the card, keyframes are renamed, @import and url() are dropped, and < is escaped so CSS can't close its own style tag.
Containmentthe app's wrapperA fixed height with overflow: clip, contain: layout paint style and isolation. Even position: fixed stays inside the card, so it can't draw a fake overlay over Home.

Data

Numbers come from the app, and they stay current

persistable reads

Every chat read tool, behind an adapter

Investigate, cashflow, transactions, detail, scenario, entities, balances, accounts, recurring, goals, wealth, forecast and agent findings. Each declares its input schema and AI scopes, which are checked again on every view. Output is made readable (formatted money, names for ids) with internal evidence stripped.

dates as meaning

“This month” stays this month

Queries save tokens such as @month_start, @days_ago:29 and @param:month.from, resolved in your timezone each view. A literal date is refused unless you asked for a fixed past period. The old approach shifted saved dates by elapsed days, so “this month” slowly became a sliding window.

params

Controls can't widen what a card reads

A request can only pick a declared option: one of the last N months, a listed period, or a listed choice. Anything else falls back to the default.

financial truth

Designers don't do money maths

Totals come from their own query. Cards show money as the app's formatted strings or through Kit.Money, which uses bigint minor units. Minor amounts become numbers only for bar lengths.

Decisions

What we could have built, and why we didn't

OptionWhy not (or why)
Keep one HTML doing two viewsthe old widgetNo. The widget was an afterthought of the page, an iframe of varying height that scrolled, loaded charts from a CDN and reloaded on theme change. And you couldn't see it on Home before pinning.
Card iframe with our CSS kitsandboxed, fixed sizeNo. It's safe, but it's an extra request, document and skeleton per card, and it still isn't native DOM.
JSON card document onlyreviewer's suggestionNot alone. It's simpler and safe, but caps how expressive a card can be. We kept its safety ideas (strict schemas, typed links, money through trusted components) and let the AI write real React.
Run AI React in the pagefastest to buildNever. The code would run with your session and could call any server action.
AI React in QuickJS on the serverchosenYes. It's as free as code, as fast and native as built-in widgets, and no AI code reaches the browser. The six presets go through the same pipeline from trusted source.
A separate artifact builderthe old routeReplaced. The artifact's chat is the chat, which gives it every read tool, durability, steering, cancel, the mic and attachments at no extra cost. Its build tracker table is gone.
Vercel Workflow for buildsNot now. Artifacts match chat exactly (after() + a request row). Surviving a deploy or crash mid-run is a later upgrade for both.

Tested live

What real runs found that unit tests didn't

bundling

The WASM moved

The production build copied QuickJS's WASM file to a path that didn't exist at runtime. Fix: load the sandbox packages from node_modules (serverExternalPackages). The card e2e test now runs against next start.

frozen dates

Six queries for six months

The first month switch came back as six queries with literal dates, so it would have frozen at November. Fix: a month param with tokens, and literal dates refused unless intended.

empty sample

Guessing field names

On the 1st of the month the sample data was empty, so the designer guessed row.categoryName and every bar read “Uncategorized”. Fix: it now also sees another option's data (last month) as a shape reference.

money

Hand-made totals

The designer summed amounts and formatted them itself. Fix: totals come from their own query, and money is shown only as app-formatted values.

Limits

What still isn't perfect

No live browser maths on Home

A slider on a card asks the server to re-render, which is fast but not 60 fps. The Page (sandboxed iframe) keeps full client-side interactivity.

Durability equals chat's

A deploy or crash mid-build loses that run. The request shows as failed, and you ask again.

A designer can still mislabel

The sandbox stops capabilities, not wrong labels. The preview, drafts and version history are how you catch and undo that.

Tailwind classes

Only classes the app already uses exist, so designed cards style themselves with style objects and scoped CSS.

Principles

The rules behind every decision

Money facts come from code

Pages and cards save queries, not numbers. Totals and formatting come from the app.

Untrusted by default

AI code runs only in a sandbox, and its output is checked before it reaches React.

See it where it will live

The preview is the real card in its Home slot. Home changes only when you publish.

Reuse, don't fork

One chat and one set of read tools. Presets and designed cards share one render pipeline.

Moneo · artifacts and Home cards · Next.js 16, React 19, Supabase, QuickJS (WASM), sucrase, postcss, Vercel AI SDK

The Home cards tab shows it in its Home slot between your own widgets, live and interactive. Pick a size, then ask for changes.

6 · publish

You decide when Home changes

Add to Home publishes that exact version. Later edits are drafts until “Update on Home”, and every version is kept to go back to.

Rendering

AI-written React that never runs in your browser

The card's code runs once on the server inside QuickJS, a JavaScript engine compiled to WASM. Its only output is a tree of plain data, { type, props, children }. The app checks that tree and draws it with its own React, so it gets your fonts and theme, switches dark mode instantly, and has no iframe.

Measured (benchmark script in the repo)

9 mscompile TSX → JS (sucrase), once at save
44 msfirst render; the WASM engine starts
1.1 mswarm render p50 (p95 2.9 ms): two charts, 12 rows
7 ms8 cards at once

The cost on Home is the data queries, which every widget already pays. Cards on one Home share reads: the same query runs once.

What a card can use

HTML and SVG (gradients, filters, clip paths), style objects, and scoped CSS with :hover, @keyframes and @media. The kit, which the app draws:

Kit.MoneyKit.ChartKit.TabsKit.ParamKit.LinkKit.Style

Tabs switch instantly in the browser. A Param (month, period or choice) re-renders the card on the server with new data in about 100 ms. Links are built by the app from a typed target.

Safety

Five walls between the model and your Home

The model writes the code, and text in your transactions could try to steer it, so we treat both the code and its output as untrusted.

LayerWhat it stops
QuickJS sandboxfresh runtime per renderNo network, files, env, timers or imports. A 1 s deadline and a 64 MB memory ceiling stop a runaway loop from stalling Home; they aren't design limits.
Tree checkallowlistOnly known HTML/SVG elements and attributes get through: no script, iframe, img, a, use, foreignObject, event handlers or dangerouslySetInnerHTML. No url() except to the card's own namespaced ids, so data can't leave through a stylesheet.
Kit schemasstrict Zod per componentUnknown props are refused. Charts take numbers and labels only, never chart-library options that accept HTML or functions. Links take a typed page plus ids, never a URL.
Scoped CSSpostcssEvery selector is prefixed with the card, keyframes are renamed, @import and url() are dropped, and < is escaped so CSS can't close its own style tag.
Containmentthe app's wrapperA fixed height with overflow: clip, contain: layout paint style and isolation. Even position: fixed stays inside the card, so it can't draw a fake overlay over Home.

Data

Numbers come from the app, and they stay current

persistable reads

Every chat read tool, behind an adapter

Investigate, cashflow, transactions, detail, scenario, entities, balances, accounts, recurring, goals, wealth, forecast and agent findings. Each declares its input schema and AI scopes, which are checked again on every view. Output is made readable (formatted money, names for ids) with internal evidence stripped.

dates as meaning

“This month” stays this month

Queries save tokens such as @month_start, @days_ago:29 and @param:month.from, resolved in your timezone each view. A literal date is refused unless you asked for a fixed past period. The old approach shifted saved dates by elapsed days, so “this month” slowly became a sliding window.

params

Controls can't widen what a card reads

A request can only pick a declared option: one of the last N months, a listed period, or a listed choice. Anything else falls back to the default.

financial truth

Designers don't do money maths

Totals come from their own query. Cards show money as the app's formatted strings or through Kit.Money, which uses bigint minor units. Minor amounts become numbers only for bar lengths.

What we could have built, and why we didn't

OptionWhy not (or why)
Keep one HTML doing two viewsthe old widgetNo. The widget was an afterthought of the page, an iframe of varying height that scrolled, loaded charts from a CDN and reloaded on theme change. And you couldn't see it on Home before pinning.
Card iframe with our CSS kitsandboxed, fixed sizeNo. It's safe, but it's an extra request, document and skeleton per card, and it still isn't native DOM.
JSON card document onlyreviewer's suggestionNot alone. It's simpler and safe, but caps how expressive a card can be. We kept its safety ideas (strict schemas, typed links, money through trusted components) and let the AI write real React.
Run AI React in the pagefastest to buildNever. The code would run with your session and could call any server action.
AI React in QuickJS on the serverchosenYes. It's as free as code, as fast and native as built-in widgets, and no AI code reaches the browser. The six presets go through the same pipeline from trusted source.
A separate artifact builderthe old routeReplaced. The artifact's chat is the chat, which gives it every read tool, durability, steering, cancel, the mic and attachments at no extra cost. Its build tracker table is gone.

Tested live

What real runs found that unit tests didn't

bundling

The WASM moved

The production build copied QuickJS's WASM file to a path that didn't exist at runtime. Fix: load the sandbox packages from node_modules (serverExternalPackages). The card e2e test now runs against next start.

frozen dates

Six queries for six months

The first month switch came back as six queries with literal dates, so it would have frozen at November. Fix: a month param with tokens, and literal dates refused unless intended.

empty sample

Guessing field names

On the 1st of the month the sample data was empty, so the designer guessed row.categoryName and every bar read “Uncategorized”. Fix: it now also sees another option's data (last month) as a shape reference.

money

Hand-made totals

The designer summed amounts and formatted them itself. Fix: totals come from their own query, and money is shown only as app-formatted values.

Limits

What still isn't perfect

No live browser maths on Home

A slider on a card asks the server to re-render, which is fast but not 60 fps. The Page (sandboxed iframe) keeps full client-side interactivity.

Durability equals chat's

A deploy or crash mid-build loses that run. The request shows as failed, and you ask again.

A designer can still mislabel

The sandbox stops capabilities, not wrong labels. The preview, drafts and version history are how you catch and undo that.

Tailwind classes

Only classes the app already uses exist, so designed cards style themselves with style objects and scoped CSS.

Principles

The rules behind every decision

Money facts come from code

Pages and cards save queries, not numbers. Totals and formatting come from the app.

Untrusted by default

AI code runs only in a sandbox, and its output is checked before it reaches React.

See it where it will live

The preview is the real card in its Home slot. Home changes only when you publish.

Reuse, don't fork

One chat and one set of read tools. Presets and designed cards share one render pipeline.

+        <rect x="700" y="260" width="340" height="190" rx="16" fill="#f0efea" stroke="#5d6170"/>

+        <path d="M200 150 V200 Q200 230 300 230 H470 V260" stroke="#5d6170" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="5 4" marker-end="url(#a)"/>
+        <text x="300" y="224" fill="#5d6170" font-size="12">preview renders the draft version</text>

+

From “add this to Home” to a card you can trust

+

Every step is a normal chat request, so it keeps going if you close the tab and shows as working when you come back.

+
1 · ask

Say it in the chat

“Add a small card with last month's total and top categories, with a month switch.”

+
2 · read

The agent reads real data

It uses the same read tools as chat, then writes queries with dates as meaning (@param:month.from), never fixed dates.

+
3 · design

Preset or its own React

If one of six shapes fits, it fills a preset. Otherwise a designer writes the card's own TSX, with any layout, several charts or custom SVG.

+
4 · check

Rendered before it's saved

It's compiled and run at S, M, L and XL with live data, and the tree is checked. Failures go back to the designer up to 3 times.

+
5 · preview

A draft, in place

The Home cards tab shows it in its Home slot between your own widgets, live and interactive. Pick a size, then ask for changes.

+
6 · publish

You decide when Home changes

Add to Home publishes that exact version. Later edits are drafts until “Update on Home”, and every version is kept to go back to.

+

AI-written React that never runs in your browser

+

The card's code runs once on the server inside QuickJS, a JavaScript engine compiled to WASM. Its only output is a tree of plain data, { type, props, children }. The app checks that tree and draws it with its own React, so it gets your fonts and theme, switches dark mode instantly, and has no iframe.

+
9 mscompile TSX → JS (sucrase), once at save

+
44 msfirst render; the WASM engine starts

+
1.1 mswarm render p50 (p95 2.9 ms): two charts, 12 rows

+

The cost on Home is the data queries, which every widget already pays. Cards on one Home share reads: the same query runs once.

+

HTML and SVG (gradients, filters, clip paths), style objects, and scoped CSS with :hover, @keyframes and @media. The kit, which the app draws:

+
Kit.MoneyKit.ChartKit.TabsKit.ParamKit.LinkKit.Style

+

Tabs switch instantly in the browser. A Param (month, period or choice) re-renders the card on the server with new data in about 100 ms. Links are built by the app from a typed target.

+

Five walls between the model and your Home

+

The model writes the code, and text in your transactions could try to steer it, so we treat both the code and its output as untrusted.
+ QuickJS sandboxfresh runtime per renderNo network, files, env, timers or imports. A 1 s deadline and a 64 MB memory ceiling stop a runaway loop from stalling Home; they aren't design limits.

+ Tree checkallowlistOnly known HTML/SVG elements and attributes get through: no script, iframe, img, a, use, foreignObject, event handlers or dangerouslySetInnerHTML. No url() except to the card's own namespaced ids, so data can't leave through a stylesheet.

+ Kit schemasstrict Zod per componentUnknown props are refused. Charts take numbers and labels only, never chart-library options that accept HTML or functions. Links take a typed page plus ids, never a URL.
+ Scoped CSSpostcssEvery selector is prefixed with the card, keyframes are renamed, @import and url() are dropped, and < is escaped so CSS can't close its own style tag.
+ Containmentthe app's wrapperA fixed height with overflow: clip, contain: layout paint style and isolation. Even position: fixed stays inside the card, so it can't draw a fake overlay over Home.

+

Numbers come from the app, and they stay current

+
persistable reads

Every chat read tool, behind an adapter

Investigate, cashflow, transactions, detail, scenario, entities, balances, accounts, recurring, goals, wealth, forecast and agent findings. Each declares its input schema and AI scopes, which are checked again on every view. Output is made readable (formatted money, names for ids) with internal evidence stripped.

+
dates as meaning

“This month” stays this month

Queries save tokens such as @month_start, @days_ago:29 and @param:month.from, resolved in your timezone each view. A literal date is refused unless you asked for a fixed past period. The old approach shifted saved dates by elapsed days, so “this month” slowly became a sliding window.

+
params

Controls can't widen what a card reads

A request can only pick a declared option: one of the last N months, a listed period, or a listed choice. Anything else falls back to the default.

+
financial truth

Designers don't do money maths

Totals come from their own query. Cards show money as the app's formatted strings or through Kit.Money, which uses bigint minor units. Minor amounts become numbers only for bar lengths.

+

What we could have built, and why we didn't

+ Keep one HTML doing two viewsthe old widgetNo. The widget was an afterthought of the page, an iframe of varying height that scrolled, loaded charts from a CDN and reloaded on theme change. And you couldn't see it on Home before pinning.
+ Card iframe with our CSS kitsandboxed, fixed sizeNo. It's safe, but it's an extra request, document and skeleton per card, and it still isn't native DOM.

+ JSON card document onlyreviewer's suggestionNot alone. It's simpler and safe, but caps how expressive a card can be. We kept its safety ideas (strict schemas, typed links, money through trusted components) and let the AI write real React.
+ Run AI React in the pagefastest to buildNever. The code would run with your session and could call any server action.

+ AI React in QuickJS on the serverchosenYes. It's as free as code, as fast and native as built-in widgets, and no AI code reaches the browser. The six presets go through the same pipeline from trusted source.

+ A separate artifact builderthe old routeReplaced. The artifact's chat is the chat, which gives it every read tool, durability, steering, cancel, the mic and attachments at no extra cost. Its build tracker table is gone.
+ Vercel Workflow for buildsNot now. Artifacts match chat exactly (after() + a request row). Surviving a deploy or crash mid-run is a later upgrade for both.

+

What real runs found that unit tests didn't

+
bundling

The WASM moved

The production build copied QuickJS's WASM file to a path that didn't exist at runtime. Fix: load the sandbox packages from node_modules (serverExternalPackages). The card e2e test now runs against next start.

+
frozen dates

Six queries for six months

The first month switch came back as six queries with literal dates, so it would have frozen at November. Fix: a month param with tokens, and literal dates refused unless intended.

+
empty sample

Guessing field names

On the 1st of the month the sample data was empty, so the designer guessed row.categoryName and every bar read “Uncategorized”. Fix: it now also sees another option's data (last month) as a shape reference.

+
money

Hand-made totals

The designer summed amounts and formatted them itself. Fix: totals come from their own query, and money is shown only as app-formatted values.

+

No live browser maths on Home

A slider on a card asks the server to re-render, which is fast but not 60 fps. The Page (sandboxed iframe) keeps full client-side interactivity.

+

Durability equals chat's

A deploy or crash mid-build loses that run. The request shows as failed, and you ask again.

+

A designer can still mislabel

The sandbox stops capabilities, not wrong labels. The preview, drafts and version history are how you catch and undo that.

+

Tailwind classes

Only classes the app already uses exist, so designed cards style themselves with style objects and scoped CSS.

+

Money facts come from code

Pages and cards save queries, not numbers. Totals and formatting come from the app.

+

Untrusted by default

AI code runs only in a sandbox, and its output is checked before it reaches React.

+

See it where it will live

The preview is the real card in its Home slot. Home changes only when you publish.

+

Reuse, don't fork

One chat and one set of read tools. Presets and designed cards share one render pipeline.
+<footer>Moneo · artifacts and Home cards · Next.js 16, React 19, Supabase, QuickJS (WASM), sucrase, postcss, Vercel AI SDK</footer>

cd C:/Users/mgsuk/.t3/worktrees/Moneo/t3-c5d7c3ec; cat > .qa/pr.md <<'EOF'
## What changes

Artifacts are now built in their **own chat**, and any part of one can become a **native Home card**. The card is previewed in its Home slot, sized (S/M/L/XL) and published by you.

- **Agent = the chat.** An artifact's conversation runs through `/api/chat` with every chat tool plus `write_page`, `card_preset`, `write_card` and `remove_card`. It has the same durability as chat: the `chat_requests` row plus `after()` keep it running when the tab closes, it resumes on reopen, and steer, cancel, mic and attachments all work. The old builder route and `artifact_builds` are removed.
- **Cards are AI-written React, rendered on the server.**
  - The designer writes `card.tsx`. Sucrase compiles it and it runs in **QuickJS (WASM)**, a fresh runtime per render, which returns a plain element tree.
  - The tree is checked (HTML/SVG allowlist, namespaced ids, no `url()` out, strict Zod per Kit component, CSS scoped with postcss), then drawn by our React inside a clipped, isolated, fixed-height box. There is no iframe, and no AI code runs in the browser.
  - The six presets are our own card code going through the same pipeline.
- **Data stays app-owned and current.**
  - Queries can use every chat read tool, through adapters that check scopes on every view.
  - Dates are saved as tokens (`@month_start`, `@param:month.from`, …). Literal dates are refused unless the user asked for a fixed past period.
  - Month, period and choice controls only accept declared options and re-render the card through `GET /api/cards/:id`.
- **Draft → publish.** Chat edits create new card versions. Home shows the published version until "Update on Home". Layout keys are now `card:<id>`.
- **Presentation:** `docs/artifact-cards-architecture.html` covers the architecture, rendering, safety, data, the decisions taken and why, what live testing found, and the limits.

## Migration

`202611010001_artifact_cards.sql` is **already applied to the dev DB**. It drops `artifact_builds` (7 status rows), adds `conversations.artifact_id`, `artifact_cards` and `artifact_card_versions` with composite workspace keys, and keeps `lib/schema.ts` aligned. Old `artifact:<id>` Home keys are simply ignored, since backward compatibility wasn't needed.

## Verification

- `npm test`: 1206 passed. `npm run lint`: clean. `npm run build`: passes.
- Card benchmark (`npx tsx scripts/bench-cards.mts`): about 1 ms warm render, 44 ms cold, 8 cards in 7 ms.
- `e2e/artifact-home.gated.spec.ts` (rewritten) passes against `next start`. It covers native preview with no iframe, size change, Add to Home, the control re-rendering on Home, and delete removing the card.
- **Live model runs** (OpenAI) built a page and card in 54–62 s and an edit in 40 s, with the month switch working on Home. Live runs found and fixed:
  - the WASM path broken by bundling
  - six literal-date queries that would freeze the card
  - empty-month sample data making the designer guess field names
  - hand-rolled money totals
  - a `ytd` period bug
- `e2e/home-dashboard.gated.spec.ts` fails on the QA workspace because "Waiting for you" sections now render above the grid. This isn't caused by this change: those sections come from existing agent-team data.

## Known limits

- Home cards have no client-side live maths; a slider re-renders on the server.
- Durability is the same as chat's: a deploy or crash mid-build loses that run.
- Hard-deleting an artifact whose chat has messages is blocked by the existing `messages` foreign key. The app only soft-deletes.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
gh pr create --base main --head t3/artifact-overview-design --title "Artifacts in their own chat, with native AI-designed Home cards" --body-file .qa/pr.md 2>&1 | tail -1
